options.text: Invite a few branch pharmacists to the next sprint reviews to try the latest increment on realistic orders and say what gets in their way.
options.rationale: The people who will use the tool are the only ones who can show whether it works in their day. Bringing them into reviews now gives the team evidence about value while three months of work can still be steered by it.

options.text: Release the current increment to two branches now and watch how pharmacists use it for their real orders, alongside their existing ordering process.
options.rationale: A small live release tests the tool against real workload, interruptions and stock patterns that no review room can reproduce. Running it alongside the existing process keeps the risk to the branches low.

options.text: Ask the head-office managers to write more detailed acceptance criteria for each story, drawing on their own knowledge of how branches place their orders.
options.rationale: The candidate tightens the definition of done but keeps the same proxies as the judges of value. More detailed criteria written without users make conformance easier to check, not value easier to see.

options.text: Keep the month-eight release date but add a dedicated user-acceptance testing phase with branch pharmacists in the sprint just before the branch rollout.
options.rationale: It does involve real users, but at the point where their feedback is most expensive to act on. The candidate treats user involvement as a final gate rather than as the feedback loop that should shape the remaining months.

options.text: Ask the product owner to survey all branch pharmacists about the ordering features they want most, and then reorder the remaining backlog by the results.
options.rationale: A survey gathers stated wishes about features nobody has seen, not evidence about whether the built tool helps. The candidate mistakes asking users about the product for letting them use it.

options.text: Have the team shadow the head-office ordering analysts for a week, since they handle branch queries and know where the current ordering process fails.
options.rationale: The analysts know the problems second-hand, and learning from them is useful context. But it adds another proxy rather than putting the product in front of the people whose work it is meant to change.

questions.explanation: Value is judged by the people who will use the product, in the conditions they will use it, and the sooner the better. Proxies such as product owners, managers and analysts can accept increments, but their acceptance is evidence of their view rather than of the product's value. Put increments in front of real users early, through reviews and small live releases, so the feedback loop measures usefulness and not just conformance.
questions.mindset: Let the people who will use the product tell you whether it works for them, early and often.

questions.stem: A building society's hybrid programme is replacing its branch teller system. The agile team releases new teller features to all 60 branches every two weeks. Branch managers report that staff are struggling to keep up: keying errors have risen 15 per cent since the releases began, and two features released last quarter are barely used because staff never had time to learn them. Which two actions best protect the value of what the team delivers?

options.text: Keep deploying every two weeks but hide new teller features behind switches, turning them on for branches in planned monthly bundles with short training notes.
options.rationale: It separates deployment from release. The team keeps its fast, low-risk engineering cadence, while branches receive change at a pace they can learn, with the support to use what arrives.

options.text: Ask branch managers to nominate staff to join release planning, so the team learns what branches can absorb and schedules changes around their busiest periods.
options.rationale: The branches' capacity to absorb change is now the constraint on value, and the people who live with it are the ones who can describe it. Bringing them into planning lets the team shape releases around that capacity instead of guessing at it.

options.text: Lengthen the team's sprints to six weeks, so that fewer releases reach branches and each one has been through more thorough testing before it is deployed.
options.rationale: The candidate fixes a problem in the receiving organisation by slowing the team's feedback loop. Longer sprints delay learning and enlarge each change without giving branches any more support to adopt it.

options.text: Pause new features until keying errors return to their earlier level, and use the team's capacity in the meantime to fix the defects that branches have reported.
options.rationale: It treats rising errors as a quality problem in the software, when the stem points to the pace of change and lack of time to learn. Pausing stops the symptom briefly and leaves the cause in place for when releases resume.

options.text: Continue releasing every two weeks, since frequent delivery is how value reaches users soonest, and ask HR to schedule extra teller training sessions each month.
options.rationale: The candidate equates deployment with delivered value. Training helps, but adding classroom time on top of fortnightly change asks branches to absorb even more, and features nobody uses still deliver nothing.

questions.explanation: Value is delivered when the receiving organisation can use what is released, not when the code is deployed. When users' capacity to absorb change becomes the constraint, separate deployment from release: keep the engineering cadence and group what users see into changes they can learn, planned with them. Slowing the team down or pushing harder on the users both miss that the bottleneck sits outside the team.
questions.mindset: Pace what users receive to what they can absorb, because features nobody uses deliver nothing.

questions.stem: Your project retrofitted insulation and heat pumps in 120 council-owned buildings, with a business case promising a 25 per cent cut in heating costs. A year after completion, the facilities director reports heating bills down 31 per cent and wants to declare the benefit exceeded. You note that the winter was unusually mild and that the council moved to a cheaper energy tariff mid-year. Which two actions would give the most reliable view of the benefit?

options.text: Measure the energy the buildings consumed rather than the money spent on it, and adjust that consumption for the mild winter using heating degree-day data for the area.
options.rationale: Measuring energy in kilowatt-hours removes the tariff change, and degree-day normalisation removes the weather. What remains is much closer to the effect of the retrofit itself, which is what the business case claimed.

options.text: Compare the change in the retrofitted buildings with the change over the same period in similar council buildings that were not retrofitted at all.
options.rationale: A comparison group experiences the same winter and the same tariff, so the difference between the two groups isolates what the retrofit added. It also catches influences nobody has thought to adjust for.

options.text: Report the 31 per cent saving as achieved, with a note explaining that the mild winter and the new tariff may have contributed to part of the reduction.
options.rationale: The candidate makes the confounders visible but still reports a figure known to include them. A footnote does not stop the headline becoming the baseline future periods are judged against.

options.text: Wait for a second full year of bills before reporting any figure, so that the effect of one unusually mild winter is averaged out of the results.
options.rationale: Another year may be mild or harsh, so averaging two winters does not reliably remove weather, and the tariff effect remains in the bills. The candidate delays the review without correcting the measure.

options.text: Ask the retrofit contractor to calculate the saving from their design models, since the models isolate the effect of the measures they installed.
options.rationale: Design models show the saving the measures were expected to produce, not what was realised in use. The candidate swaps a confounded measurement for a forecast, which cannot confirm a benefit.

options.text: Survey the people working in the buildings on comfort and heating use, to confirm the fall in bills reflects the retrofit rather than changed behaviour.
options.rationale: Behaviour is one possible influence, but a survey cannot quantify the weather or the tariff, which are the two known distortions here. The candidate investigates a minor confounder and leaves the major ones in place.

questions.explanation: A benefit can be claimed only to the extent that other causes have been removed from the measure. Measure the physical quantity the change affects rather than a money figure that prices also move, normalise for known external drivers, and where possible compare with a group that did not receive the change. Reporting a headline that includes windfalls overstates value and sets a baseline later periods cannot meet.
questions.mindset: Before claiming a benefit, strip out what would have happened anyway.

questions.stem: A predictive project is delivering a fleet-telematics system for a water utility, with fuel and maintenance benefits expected to appear over two years. Match each benefits-management task to the person who should own it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Keeping the benefits register current during delivery, and handing over the agreed measures and baselines when the project closes.
Changing depot working practices so that drivers act on the route data, then reporting fuel savings every quarter for two years after closure.
Deciding at a stage gate whether the forecast benefits still justify the spending that remains on the project.

options.text: The project manager
options.rationale: During delivery the project manager maintains the benefits register and makes sure the measures and baselines are ready to hand over. The role ends at closure, which is why the handover itself is part of the task.

options.text: The benefit owner in fleet operations
options.rationale: Benefits appear in the business, through changed working practices, long after the project has gone. The benefit owner controls those practices and stays in post to report, so both the change and the reporting sit with them.

options.text: The project sponsor
options.rationale: Whether the investment is still worth continuing is a decision about the business case, which the sponsor owns. The project manager supplies the forecast; the sponsor decides what it means for the remaining spend.

options.text: The telematics supplier
options.rationale: Not used. The supplier delivers the system and may offer dashboards that show savings, but it controls neither the utility's working practices nor its investment decisions, so it cannot own any of these tasks.

questions.explanation: Benefits management assigns each task to the role that controls the thing being managed. The project manager controls delivery and so maintains the record and prepares the handover; the business controls the working practices through which benefits appear, and so owns realising and reporting them after closure; the sponsor owns the investment, and so decides whether it is still justified. A task given to someone who does not control its outcome tends to be reported on rather than achieved.
questions.mindset: Give each benefits task to the person who controls the result, not the person who is nearest to the data.

questions.stem: An agile team at an online travel agency chooses how to put each change in front of customers so that its value can be confirmed without putting revenue at risk. Match each situation to the release approach that fits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A new hotel-ranking algorithm could lower bookings if it is wrong, so the team wants it shown first to two per cent of visitors, widening only while bookings hold.
A rebuilt search service must cope with peak-season traffic, but its launch is six weeks away, so the team wants it running on live traffic without customers seeing its results.
Two wordings for the booking button are ready, and the product owner wants to know which of them produces more completed bookings.

options.text: Canary release
options.rationale: A canary exposes a change to a small share of real traffic and widens it in steps while the key measure holds. If bookings fall, only a small group was affected and the change is withdrawn cheaply.

options.text: Dark launch
options.rationale: A dark launch runs new code in production on real load while customers still see the existing results. It proves the service copes before anyone depends on it, without revealing it ahead of the planned launch.

options.text: A/B test
options.rationale: When the question is which of two versions performs better, an A/B test splits traffic between them at the same time and compares the outcome measure. Running them together removes the effects of season and demand from the comparison.

options.text: Single release to all customers on one date
options.rationale: Not used. Releasing to everyone at once gives the widest exposure and the least chance to learn before value is at risk. None of the three situations needs everyone switched over on the same day.

questions.explanation: Release approaches differ in what they let the team learn and how much value they put at risk while learning it. Progressive exposure suits a change that might do harm, production running without exposure suits a question about capacity or stability, and a simultaneous split suits a choice between versions. Choosing the approach from the question being asked keeps each release both a delivery of value and a test of it.
questions.mindset: Decide what a release needs to prove, then expose customers only as far as proving it requires.

questions.stem: A city council's hybrid programme is digitising its waste, housing and finance services, and the finance team is classifying the benefits before they go into the business case. Complete each sentence with the category that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Route-planning software lets the existing 40 refuse crews cover 3,000 new homes being built, so the four extra crews that would otherwise be hired are not needed. This benefit is
An online repairs service lets the council end a £250,000 call-handling contract when it expires next year. This benefit is
Finance officers each save four hours a week on reconciliations, but no posts are cut and the time goes to answering residents' queries faster. This benefit is

options.text: cost avoidance, because it prevents spending that would otherwise arise rather than reducing today's budget
options.rationale: The four crews are not in today's budget; they are a cost the council would have had to take on. Preventing that future cost is avoidance, and it cannot be removed from any current budget line.

options.text: a cash-releasing saving, because money can be taken out of a budget line once it is realised
options.rationale: Ending a contract the council currently pays for removes a real sum from a real budget. That is what makes a saving cash-releasing, and it is the only category here that frees money for other uses.

options.text: a non-cash-releasing efficiency, because time is freed for other work but the budget does not fall
options.rationale: The officers' time is worth something and is put to better use, but the pay bill stays the same. Counting it as a cash saving would let the business case promise money that never leaves the budget.

options.text: a revenue gain, because the council collects more income as a direct result of the change
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three changes brings in new income; each either avoids, removes or redeploys cost. Calling a cost benefit revenue confuses where the value shows up in the accounts.

questions.explanation: Benefits are classified by where their value shows up, because the category decides what can be done with it. Only cash-releasing savings can be taken out of a budget; cost avoidance prevents future spending that was never budgeted; non-cash-releasing efficiencies free capacity that is redeployed rather than banked. Adding the three together as if they were one kind of money overstates what the business case can actually return.
questions.mindset: Know where a benefit will show up in the accounts before adding it to anything else.

questions.stem: A meal-kit company's product owner is weighing a family-plan feature that costs £120,000 to build. If families take it up, it earns £400,000 net margin in its first year; if not, £20,000. She judges take-up 40 per cent likely. A four-week fake-door test costing £15,000 would show reliably whether families take it up, and she would build only if they do. Ignore the delay and any value beyond the first year. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Expected first-year net value of building now without the test, in £
blanks.rationale: Expected margin is 0.4 × 400,000 + 0.6 × 20,000 = 160,000 + 12,000 = £172,000. Subtracting the £120,000 build cost leaves an expected net value of £52,000.

blanks.label: Expected first-year net value of testing first and building only if families take it up, after paying for the test, in £
blanks.rationale: With 40 per cent probability the test shows take-up and the build earns 400,000 − 120,000 = £280,000. With 60 per cent probability nothing is built and the value is zero. That gives 0.4 × 280,000 = £112,000, less the £15,000 test, which is £97,000.

blanks.label: The most it would be worth paying for the test, in £
blanks.rationale: Before the test's cost, testing first is worth £112,000 against £52,000 for building blind. The difference, £60,000, is the value of knowing the answer before committing, so any test cheaper than that is worth running.

questions.explanation: An experiment is worth running when its answer could change the decision and the cost of deciding wrongly is larger than the cost of finding out. The value of the information is the expected value of the decision made with it minus the expected value made without it, and that figure is the ceiling on what the test should cost. When most of the downside comes from building something nobody uses, a cheap test that can prevent the build is usually worth more than it first appears.
questions.mindset: Price what you would learn before you price what you would build.

questions.stem: A hybrid programme is building a new central library to a fixed opening date. The agile team building its online room-booking service has time for only one slice of its story map before opening day, and the library wants residents able to book and pay for rooms from that day. Each slice lists the stories it contains. Select the slice that should form the first release.

graphic.title: Story map for room booking, with four candidate release slices
graphic.caption: Select a slice. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between slices, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Slice A — search rooms by date; book one slot; pay by card; receive an email confirmation
regions.rationale: This is the only slice that crosses every step of the journey, so on opening day a resident can actually find, book, pay for and confirm a room. Each step is basic, but a thin complete journey delivers value where a rich partial one delivers none.

regions.label: Slice B — search by date, capacity, equipment and accessibility; compare rooms side by side; save favourite rooms
regions.rationale: Rich searching is valuable, and the accessibility filter makes it tempting, but a resident who finds the perfect room still cannot book or pay for it. The candidate perfects the first step of the journey at the cost of the rest.

regions.label: Slice C — pay by card, invoice, account or voucher; split payment across a group; automatic refunds
regions.rationale: Payment matters to the library's income, which is why a candidate may start here, but with no way to search or book there is nothing to pay for. Depth in one step does not add up to a usable service.

regions.label: Slice D — book recurring weekly slots; change and cancel bookings; join waiting lists; receive text reminders
regions.rationale: These are the features regular users will value most later, so the slice looks customer-focused, but it assumes a booking journey that does not yet exist. It builds refinements before the basic service they refine.

questions.explanation: A first release earns value only if a user can complete the journey it supports, so it is cut horizontally across every step of the story map, taking the simplest story under each. Richer stories in any single step wait for later slices. When time is fixed, the trade is between depth and completeness, and a thin end-to-end journey beats a deep partial one because a partial journey delivers nothing usable.
questions.mindset: Make the whole journey work simply before making any part of it work well.
